section_summary: Pages 444-485 conclude a retrospective account by former prime minister Fumimaro Konoe of the deteriorating Japanese-American negotiations in 1941, Yōsuke Matsuoka’s resistance, the occupation of French Indochina, the unsuccessful proposal for a Konoe-Roosevelt meeting, and the Cabinet crisis that brought Hideki Tojo to power. Konoe emphasizes Emperor Hirohito’s preference for diplomacy and attributes the failure of negotiations partly to divided authority between the civilian government and the military high command. Pages 486-492 contain a State Department forwarding note and Owen Lattimore’s February 1946 observations on occupation policy in Japan, postwar conditions in China, and emerging nationalist tensions in Inner Mongolia.

subfiles.title: Konoe memoir on Japanese-American negotiations and the fall of his Cabinet
subfiles.about: Konoe recounts the diplomatic and political crises of 1941 that ended his premiership and preceded Hideki Tojo's accession.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion describes German and Matsuoka opposition to accommodation with the United States, the effect of the German-Soviet war, Japan's advance into French Indochina, and the resulting American economic measures. Konoe details his unsuccessful effort to arrange a personal meeting with President Roosevelt, Emperor Hirohito's repeated preference for diplomacy, and the fatal disagreement with the Army over withdrawing troops from China. It closes with the resignation of the Konoe Cabinet, Tojo's selection as prime minister, and Konoe's criticism of the institutional separation between civilian diplomacy and the military supreme command.

subfiles.title: Office memorandum forwarding Owen Lattimore's observations
subfiles.about: Vincent forwards an Owen Lattimore memorandum concerning Japan, China, and Mongolia to Under Secretary Acheson.
subfiles.summary: Vincent states that Lattimore prepared the attached memorandum at his request. He particularly recommends its opening discussion of Japan while also calling attention to its observations on China and Mongolia.

subfiles.title: Recent Observations in Japan and China
subfiles.about: Lattimore records political observations made while accompanying Ambassador Pauley's Reparations Mission in Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Lattimore argues that the occupation of Japan must move from disarmament to creating durable democratic interests, including explicit repeal of the Meiji Rescript on Education. He contrasts Japanese-maintained economic order in occupied Chinese cities with the production collapse, inflation, and political exactions that accompanied the Nationalist return. Drawing on a conversation with Teh Wang, he predicts a locally driven Inner Mongolian secession movement and recommends American specialists, consulates, and representation in Mongolia to improve political intelligence.
